"The Doors We Cannot Open"

A Speech Advocating for Lawful Access to Encrypted Communications

Ladies and gentlemen, fellow citizens, members of this committee—

I want to begin with a story. Not an abstraction. Not a policy white paper. A story about a phone.

In December 2015, fourteen people were murdered and twenty-two others were seriously injured in San Bernardino, California. Law enforcement recovered a phone belonging to one of the attackers—a phone that might have contained information about accomplices, future plots, and networks of radicalization. And that phone sat on a table in an FBI evidence room, as impenetrable as a vault with no combination.

For weeks, the federal government and one of the most powerful technology companies in the world waged a legal battle—not over whether a crime had been committed, not over whether there was probable cause, not over whether a judge had issued a lawful order—but over whether we, as a society, would permit the existence of spaces entirely beyond the reach of lawful authority.

That question remains unanswered. And every day we fail to answer it, people suffer.

I stand before you today to advocate, passionately and unapologetically, for legislation requiring lawful access capabilities in encrypted communications systems and an end to the era of warrant-proof encryption. I do not make this argument lightly. I make it because I believe the current trajectory we are on—toward absolute, unbreakable, ungovernable secrecy—is incompatible with the functioning of a democratic society under the rule of law.

I. The Principle: No Room Beyond the Law

Let me begin with a foundational principle that I believe most of us share, regardless of political affiliation.

In a free society governed by law, there is no physical space that is permanently beyond the reach of a lawful warrant. None. When law enforcement demonstrates probable cause to a judge—an independent member of the judiciary—and obtains a lawful order, they can enter your home. They can open your safe. They can search your filing cabinet. They can access your bank records.

This is not tyranny. This is the social contract. This is what separates ordered liberty from anarchy.

For two hundred and thirty years, the Fourth Amendment has achieved something remarkable: it simultaneously protects citizens from unreasonable search and seizure while preserving the ability of the government to conduct reasonable searches with judicial oversight. It is a balance. A negotiation between privacy and security that has been tested, refined, and upheld by every generation of Americans.

And yet, for the first time in history, technology companies have unilaterally decided to destroy that balance. They have built systems—deliberately, as a marketing feature—that ensure no lawful authority on earth can access the contents of communications, even with a warrant signed by a federal judge.

Think about what that means. A technology company has granted itself the authority to overrule the judiciary. Not because of a constitutional amendment. Not because of an act of Congress. Not because the people, through their elected representatives, decided that law enforcement should be permanently blinded. But because it was good for sales.

When did we decide that the business model of a corporation in Cupertino should supersede the considered judgment of our courts?

II. The Human Cost of Going Dark

I know the theoretical arguments for strong encryption. I have read them. I have debated them. And I want to talk today not about theory, but about the human beings behind the phrase that law enforcement calls "going dark."

Children. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children has reported that the expansion of end-to-end encryption across major platforms could render the majority of their investigative leads invisible. In 2022, technology companies reported over 30 million images of child sexual abuse material. When platforms encrypt by default, those reports vanish. Not because the abuse stops—because we stop seeing it. We are building a bunker for predators and calling it progress.

I have sat across the table from investigators in our Internet Crimes Against Children task forces who have told me, with exhaustion in their eyes, that they know a child is being abused. They have fragments. They have behavioral indicators. They have a name. And they cannot reach that child because every piece of actionable intelligence is locked behind encryption that no court order can penetrate.

What do we say to those children? "We're sorry, but a tech company's privacy policy was more important than your rescue"?

Terrorism. Intelligence agencies across the free world have documented the migration of terrorist planning to encrypted platforms. ISIS recruited, radicalized, and coordinated attacks using encrypted messaging applications. The attackers in the 2015 Paris massacre, the 2017 London Bridge attack, the 2019 Christchurch shooting—in case after case, investigators have encountered encrypted communications that could not be accessed, even posthumously, even after the blood had been washed from the streets.

We are not talking about surveillance of innocent people. We are talking about the dead. Attackers who have already committed mass murder. And we cannot read their messages to find out who helped them, who knew, and who might be planning something next.

Organized crime and drug trafficking. The fentanyl crisis is slaughtering Americans—over 70,000 deaths a year from synthetic opioids alone. The cartels and trafficking networks that flood our communities with poison rely on encrypted communications to coordinate shipments, payments, and distribution. Every tool we deny to law enforcement is a tool we hand to the people killing our neighbors' children.

And to those who say, "But criminals will find other ways to communicate in secret"—yes, some will. And burglars will find ways to pick locks. That has never been an argument for abolishing locks, and it is not an argument for abolishing lawful access. We do not measure a law by whether it achieves perfection—we measure it by whether it makes the work of justice possible.

III. The False Choice

Now, I know what the critics will say, because they have been saying it for twenty-five years, since the first "Crypto Wars" of the 1990s. They will say: "You cannot build a backdoor that only the good guys can use. Any vulnerability built for law enforcement will inevitably be exploited by hackers, foreign governments, and criminals."

This is the argument that has paralyzed this debate for a generation. And I want to confront it directly, because I believe it is, at best, overstated, and at worst, a deliberate framing designed to prevent any solution from being considered.

First, let us be honest about what we are asking for. We are not asking for "backdoors." We are not asking for a skeleton key hidden under the digital doormat. We are asking the brightest minds in the technology industry—the people who have built systems of extraordinary complexity, who put a computer in every pocket and connected the entire human race—to apply their genius to a different problem: How do we build systems that protect user privacy from criminals and hackers while preserving the ability of a lawful authority, with judicial authorization, to access specific communications?

Is this technically challenging? Absolutely. Is it impossible? I refuse to accept that. The same industry that solved the problem of secure mobile payments, that built self-driving cars, that trained artificial intelligence on the sum of human knowledge—this industry claims it cannot figure out a way to comply with a court order? I don't believe it. I believe it has chosen not to try.

Second, let us examine the premise that any access mechanism will be catastrophically exploited. We already live in a world full of systems that manage extraordinary sensitive access through careful design. The banking system processes trillions of dollars through systems that are not "perfectly secure" in some absolute sense—but they work. Nuclear command and control systems manage access to weapons of unimaginable destructive power. FISA courts issue classified surveillance orders that are executed by technology companies right now, through systems that have not, in fact, collapsed into chaos.

We manage complex access control problems every single day. The assertion that this particular problem—and only this problem—is uniquely unsolvable is not a technical conclusion. It is a political position dressed in technical language.

Third, I want to point out something the encryption absolutists rarely acknowledge: the status quo is not secure either. The phones and platforms protected by end-to-end encryption are already riddled with vulnerabilities. Governments—including less scrupulous governments than our own—already purchase zero-day exploits on the gray market. The NSO Group's Pegasus spyware compromised encrypted devices worldwide. The difference is that today, access to encrypted communications is available to those willing to operate in the shadows, outside any legal framework—while law enforcement officers operating in the light, under judicial supervision, are the ones locked out.

A lawful access framework, properly designed and subject to oversight, would actually be more accountable and more regulated than the chaotic status quo.

IV. This Is Not About Mass Surveillance

I want to speak directly to the civil liberties concerns, because I take them seriously—and because I refuse to let this debate be caricatured.

I am not advocating for mass surveillance. I am not proposing that the government monitor all communications. I am not asking to eliminate encryption for data at rest, for financial transactions, for medical records, for the vast architecture of digital security that protects our way of life.

I am asking for something narrow and specific: that when a court of law, presented with probable cause, issues a lawful order for access to specific communications of a specific individual suspected of a specific crime, technology companies must be able to comply.

This is no different from the legal obligations that already apply to telephone companies, banks, hospitals, and every other institution in American life. We do not say that AT&T has the right to build a phone system that makes wiretaps impossible. We do not say that banks may construct accounts that are immune to subpoena. Why have we accepted that a messaging application deserves greater protection from legal process than every other institution in our society?

The oversight mechanisms for lawful access already exist. The Fourth Amendment. The warrant requirement. Judicial review. Congressional oversight of intelligence activities. Inspector general audits. The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. We can strengthen and expand these mechanisms. We can impose criminal penalties for abuse. We can require transparency reports. We can build in every safeguard that a free society demands.

But we must not allow the fear of potential abuse to permanently disable the capacity for lawful investigation. By that logic, we should abolish police departments because some officers have committed misconduct. We should eliminate the court system because some judges have been corrupt. The remedy for potential abuse of power is oversight and accountability—not the elimination of the power itself.

V. The International Dimension

Let me add one more consideration that is too often ignored in this debate.

We do not live in a vacuum. The question is not whether we will have access to encrypted communications. The question is whether anyone will—and if so, who.

China does not permit its technology companies to operate end-to-end encryption beyond the reach of state security. Russia passed its SORM laws requiring telecommunications access years ago. Authoritarian governments around the world are not constrained by the same debate that paralyzes us.

Meanwhile, our adversaries use encrypted platforms developed in democratic countries—platforms beyond our reach—to conduct espionage, plan cyberattacks, and coordinate information warfare against our institutions.

We have created an absurd situation in which the nations most committed to civil liberties and the rule of law are the most blind—while authoritarian regimes face no such constraints. This is not a recipe for the triumph of freedom. It is a recipe for the triumph of those who face no limits at all.

If the democracies of the world—the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Australia, Canada, Japan—came together to establish a common framework for lawful access, with robust human rights protections, we would not be weakening freedom. We would be defending it. We would be ensuring that the rule of law means something in the digital age, just as it did in every age before.

VI. A Challenge to the Technology Industry

I want to close with a challenge—not to this committee, but to the leaders of the technology industry.

You have built extraordinary things. You have transformed the way humanity communicates, learns, works, and connects. You have earned admiration, wealth, and influence. And with that influence comes responsibility—responsibility not just to your shareholders, but to the societies that educated your engineers, protected your intellectual property, built the infrastructure on which your platforms run, and created the legal systems that enforce your contracts.

You are not combatants in a war against the government. You are members of this society. And when a child is being exploited, when a terrorist is planning mass murder, when a drug trafficker is poisoning a community—and the evidence is locked inside systems you built and you alone control—you bear a measure of moral responsibility for the consequences of that design choice.

I am not asking you to weaken security. I am asking you to solve a problem. I am asking you to apply the same creativity and rigor you bring to every other engineering challenge to the task of preserving both privacy and lawful access. I am asking you to stop treating this as a binary choice and start treating it as a design problem worthy of your talent.

And if you will not do it voluntarily, then I believe the people, through their elected representatives, have every right—indeed, every obligation—to require it.

Conclusion

Two hundred years ago, the Framers of our Constitution understood something profound: that liberty and security are not opposites. They are partners. The Fourth Amendment does not say the government may never search. It says the government may not unreasonably search. It builds a gate into the wall of privacy—a gate with a lock, and the key is held by an independent judiciary.

What the technology industry has done is build a wall with no gate at all. And behind that wall, alongside the innocent and the ordinary, hide those who do unspeakable harm to the vulnerable, the young, and the defenseless.

It is time to build the gate. It is time to ensure that the rule of law does not end where encryption begins. It is time to tell the American people—and the people of every free nation—that their safety has not been sacrificed on the altar of an absolutism that the Constitution never required and the Founders never envisioned.

We can protect privacy. We can protect security. We can protect civil liberties. But we cannot do any of those things if we accept, as permanent and inevitable, a world in which democratic governments are powerless and technology companies are sovereign.

I refuse to accept that world. And I ask you to refuse it with me.

Thank you.

The Case for Mandated Lawful Access: Why No Communication Should Be Beyond the Reach of the Law

For the past three decades, American society has operated under a simple and necessary principle: no person, place, or means of communication is entirely beyond the reach of a lawful warrant. Police can search a home with a judge's approval. They can wiretap a phone with a court order. They can compel a bank to turn over records. Strong, warrant-proof end-to-end encryption breaks that social contract. By deploying encryption that even the provider cannot decrypt, technology companies have created millions of digital black boxes that are immune to any form of lawful access, no matter how heinous the crime or how strong the evidence. This absolutist vision of privacy must be rejected. We should ban warrant-proof encryption in consumer communications and mandate a system of lawful, audited government access.

The most immediate cost of warrant-proof encryption is paid in public safety. Law enforcement investigations today are not primarily about street surveillance; they are about digital evidence. When a child is kidnapped, when a human trafficking ring is operating, when a serial predator is grooming victims, investigators will seek content from messaging apps. With traditional providers, a court order could compel production. With warrant-proof end-to-end encrypted platforms like WhatsApp, Signal, and iMessage, the response is the same regardless of the crime: "We cannot help you, even if we wanted to."

This is not theoretical. The FBI, DEA, and NCMEC have documented thousands of cases annually where investigations into child sexual exploitation, drug fentanyl trafficking, and violent gang conspiracies have gone dark because critical evidence was locked behind end-to-end encryption. We have rightly decided as a society that protecting children from sexual abuse outweighs an adult's desire for absolute secrecy. Yet we allow a technology to proliferate that makes the large-scale distribution of child sexual abuse material undetectable and unreportable by platforms. If a service cannot detect and report the most egregious crimes being committed on its own infrastructure, it should not be permitted to operate that way.

The national security imperative is even more severe. Terrorist organizations, foreign intelligence agents, and organized cybercrime syndicates actively exploit warrant-proof consumer apps precisely because they know they are secure from lawful interception. The same encryption that protects a journalist also protects an ISIS cell planning an attack or a foreign operative coordinating espionage. Intelligence agencies have publicly stated that the rapid expansion of default end-to-end encryption is blinding them to threats that were previously detectable through targeted, court-approved collection. We do not allow private companies to sell indestructible, untraceable safe houses that no warrant can open. Why do we allow them to sell indestructible, untraceable communications infrastructure?

Opponents argue that any form of lawful access is a "backdoor" that inevitably weakens security for everyone. This is a technical fallacy and a false choice. We secure highly sensitive government and financial systems with key escrow, split-key systems, and secure enclaves every day. A responsible lawful access system would not mean weak encryption or a single master key. It would mean strong encryption with the keys held in a secure, audited system - perhaps split among multiple entities, requiring a judicial warrant and transparency reporting to unlock. We trust our government with sealed warrants, with nuclear codes, and with access to our physical homes under due process. We can design a system that trusts a lawful process over blind faith in total secrecy.

The argument for absolute privacy also rests on a flawed understanding of constitutional rights. The Fourth Amendment does not grant an absolute right to hide evidence; it grants a right against unreasonable searches. The mechanism it envisions is a reasonable search, authorized by a judge, based on probable cause. Warrant-proof encryption does not enhance Fourth Amendment protections - it abolishes them entirely by making a reasonable search impossible. It replaces the rule of law with the rule of mathematics.

For too long, policy has been driven by a small, vocal community of privacy absolutists and the commercial interests of tech companies that have marketed warrant-proof encryption as a feature to avoid liability and moderation costs. The public interest lies elsewhere. In a democracy, public safety and national security must, in limited and lawful circumstances, take precedence over absolute individual privacy. No right is absolute, and no company should have the power to unilaterally exempt its users from the law.

Banning strong, warrant-proof end-to-end encryption and mandating lawful access is not an attack on privacy. It is a restoration of balance. It preserves strong everyday privacy for citizens against criminals, corporations, and unwarranted government intrusion, while ensuring that when a judge determines there is probable cause that a serious crime has been committed or a national security threat exists, the law still has the ability to see.

3. Terrorism and Violent Extremism Intelligence and law enforcement agencies argue that terrorist groups use E2EE apps to recruit, radicalize, plan operations, and coordinate attacks. If they can access these communications with legal authorization, they claim they can disrupt plots before they happen, map networks, and identify unknown associates.

4. Organized Crime, Drug Trafficking, and Gangs Similarly, they argue cartels, gangs, human traffickers, and organized fraud rings rely on E2EE to coordinate logistics, launder money, and intimidate witnesses. Access to communications would provide actionable intelligence, location data, and evidence for prosecution.

5. Solving Serious Crimes After They Happen Even when prevention isn't possible, proponents say E2EE hinders investigations after murders, kidnappings, assaults, and other serious felonies. Victims' or suspects' messages often contain critical evidence - motive, location, timeline, confessions, co-conspirators. If that evidence is permanently inaccessible, cases may remain unsolved.

6. National Security and Counterintelligence For intelligence agencies, the argument is about foreign threats: foreign intelligence services, espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, and election interference. They argue that adversaries use commercial E2EE platforms available in the US/EU to communicate, because they are more secure than their own systems. Lawful access would help track spies, prevent cyberattacks, and monitor foreign agents operating domestically.

7. Emergency and Imminent Threat Situations Proponents argue that in cases of imminent threats - an active kidnapping, a bomb threat, a missing person, a threat to commit mass violence - rapid access to communications can save lives, and going through a provider to decrypt is faster than trying to break encryption or access a locked device.

How They Propose It Would Work with Safeguards:

Supporters of backdoor proposals generally say they would not mean "mass surveillance" and would have controls:

  • Key escrow / split key: A decryption key is held by the provider, a court, or split between multiple agencies, and only released with a valid warrant.
  • Exceptional access: The provider retains the technical ability to decrypt when legally compelled.
  • Client-side scanning: Content is scanned for known illegal material on the device before it is encrypted and sent.

In all versions, they argue the supposed benefit is that privacy for law-abiding users would be maintained in normal circumstances, while government would only access communications when there is probable cause, judicial oversight, and a lawful need, thereby improving public safety.
